title: Flux product
text:
NoteSummary



The flux product combines the fluxes from the flux post-processing chain with the meteo data and, if relevant, the management data. Its timestamps are TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE in CET.

title: Flux product
text:
Variables to include
Variables widely used in ecosystem research, if available:

Fluxes: NEE, GPP, RECO, LE, H, with flags that separate measured from gap-filled values.
Meteo: TA, SW_IN, SW_OUT, LW_IN, LW_OUT, PPFD, RH, PA, PREC, SWC, TS, VPD.
Energy balance closure: G and NETRAD.

title: Flux product
text:
Sharing with FLUXNET
The L1 fluxes and the meteo data are also shared with FLUXNET, which runs its own processing. See Sharing with FLUXNET.
To be written.

title: Conventions
text:
NoteSummary



Local time in all steps is CET without daylight saving time, and the database stores timestamps in UTC, at the end of each period. Meteo variables are named VAR_H_V_R, each variable in the database carries a data version, and missing values in files for EddyPro and FLUXNET are -9999.

title: Conventions
text:
Timestamps

Local time: CET (UTC+1), all year, without daylight saving time.
Database: timestamps mark the end of the averaging period (TIMESTAMP_END), stored in UTC. Data are converted to UTC on upload and back to CET on download.
EddyPro output: TIMESTAMP_END.
diive: works internally with the middle of the period (TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE).
Flux products: TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE, CET. 09:15 covers 09:00 to 09:30. With end timestamps, a daily sum would count the record ending at midnight to the next day.
FLUXNET upload: TIMESTAMP_START and TIMESTAMP_END, format YYYYMMDDhhmm, local standard time. See Sharing with FLUXNET.

title: Conventions
text:
Variable names
Meteo variables are named VAR_H_V_R:








Part
Meaning
Examples

variable, mostly FLUXNET codes
TA, SWC, TS


H
horizontal position
T1 tower, M1 mast, GF1 grassland floor, FF1 forest floor


V

35, 1.5, 0.10

Examples: TA_T1_35_1, SWC_FF1_0.10_1, TS_GF2_0.50_1.
The position is read from the end of the name, because some names carry extra parts.
Campbell loggers do not allow . in names and use x instead, e.g. 0x02.
No special characters such as umlauts in variable, site, file or folder names.
Sites: CC-SSS, e.g. CH-DAV in Swiss FluxNet. The official FLUXNET identifier is written CH-Dav.
Other formats: FLUXNET and EddyPro use numbers for the position, e.g. TA_1_1_1. diive renames the variables for these formats, see Biomet data.

Source: Swiss FluxNet naming convention

Missing values

Files for EddyPro and FLUXNET: -9999.
rECord raw data files: "NAN".
Database and diive: empty values (NaN), no code.

title: L3.1 · Storage correction
text:
NoteSummary



L3.1 adds the storage term to the fluxes, and the CO2 flux becomes NEE. The storage term comes from profile measurements or, without them, from the one-point storage term of EddyPro.



NEE: CO2 flux + CO2 storage term. The name changes from FC to NEE.
Other fluxes (LE, H, N2O, CH4): the flux + its storage term. They keep their name, so the suffix _L3.1 marks them as storage-corrected, e.g. LE_L3.1.
Storage term: ideally from profile measurements. Without them, the one-point storage term that EddyPro calculates in the L1 run.
Missing storage terms: without a storage term, the flux record is lost. Gap-filling the storage term keeps these records.
No flags are used in this step.
Grasslands: the storage term is normally negligible. It matters for forests.

title: Meteo screening
text:
NoteSummary



A diive notebook screens each meteo variable from the raw bucket with outlier tests and corrections, and resamples it to 30 min. The screened data are uploaded to the processed bucket with the data version meteoscreening_diive.
The raw data reach the database with dataflow.

title: Meteo screening
text:
Steps

The variable is downloaded from the raw bucket, in local time.
The data are plotted. Without obvious outliers, the corrections or the resampling come next.
The outlier tests the variable needs run one at a time. Each test shows a preview; addflag() keeps its flag.
The flags are combined into the overall flag QCF.
Corrections are applied, if needed.
Optional: the radiation data are correlated with potential radiation, day by day, to find time shifts.
The data are resampled to 30 min.
The data are uploaded to the processed bucket, then downloaded again to check them.

title: Meteo screening
text:
Outlier tests
Each test flags a record with 0 (ok) or 2 (outlier). Some tests can run separately for day and night; day and night follow from the site coordinates.







Test
Flags




Manual removal
single timestamps or date ranges, given in local time


Hampel filter
spikes far from the median in a moving window


z-score
values far from the mean of the whole period


Rolling z-score
values far from the mean in a moving window


Local SD
values far from the median in a moving window, in standard deviations


Increments z-score
unusual jumps between neighbouring records


Local outlier factor
a set fraction of the records; slow on high-resolution data


Absolute limits
values outside a minimum and maximum


Trim low
values below a limit, and the same number of the highest values


Missing values
missing records, so that they count in QCF



When the resolution of the data changes, e.g. from 10 min to 1 min, the moving-window tests run on each period separately.

title: Meteo screening
text:
Overall flag QCF

Combines the test flags: 0 good, 1 marginal, 2 bad. See QCF.
Records with QCF 2 are removed before the resampling.

title: Meteo screening
text:
Corrections

Radiation offset (SW_IN, PPFD): subtracts each day’s mean nighttime value, then sets nighttime values to 0.
Relative humidity above 100 %: subtracts the daily offset above 100 %, then caps the remaining values at 100 %.
Other: values beyond a threshold set to the threshold, date ranges set to a constant, or a fixed value removed, e.g. a stuck reading.

title: Meteo screening
text:
Resampling

Target: 30 min, with TIMESTAMP_END.
Aggregation: time-weighted mean, or sum for variables that add up over the interval, e.g. precipitation.
Minimum coverage: kept records must cover a set fraction of the 30 min (the notebook uses 50 %). Otherwise the value is missing.

title: Meteo screening
text:
Upload

The screened data keep the variable name of the raw data, with the data version meteoscreening_diive.
Older screened data have the data version meteoscreening_mst, from the deprecated MeteoScreeningTool (MST). They are not corrected for everything, so problems can remain. Both versions are merged and checked in additional meteo for dataset.
Grafana: the screened data also appear in the Grafana dashboards, where both data versions can be shown next to each other.
The flags stay in the notebook and are not uploaded.
An upload replaces the screened data of the same variable and period. The raw data are not changed.

See Conventions for timestamps and data versions.

title: L4.1 · Gap-filling
text:
NoteSummary



L4.1 fills the gaps in the quality-controlled fluxes, using the meteo drivers, and tree-based models have also used management data. MDS is the default for NEE, water and energy fluxes, and random forest works well for N2O and CH4.

title: L4.1 · Gap-filling
text:
Methods

MDS (marginal distribution sampling): the default method for NEE, water and energy fluxes, with SW_IN, TA and VPD as drivers (Reichstein et al., 2005).
N2O and CH4: there is no agreed method. Random forest approaches work well (Maier et al., 2022).
Long-term random forest (diive): one model per year, trained on that year and its two neighbouring years. The first and last year use the two closest years.
XGBoost (diive): can also be used for the gap-filling. To be written.
Exceptions: where the random forest does poorly, e.g. right after a strong disturbance, MDS can fill that period instead.

title: L4.1 · Gap-filling
text:
Random forest features

Drivers per flux: e.g. air temperature, radiation and VPD for NEE, LE and H; soil temperature, soil water content and precipitation for N2O and CH4.
Lagged variants: e.g. the mean over the preceding 3 hours, or that mean shifted back by 3, 6, 9 and 12 hours.
Time since an event: the number of records since the last precipitation or management event. See Management data.
Timestamp information: e.g. year, season, month, day of year, hour.
Feature reduction: a random variable is added as a feature. Features less important than it are removed.
Importance: permutation importance, not the default Gini importance, which can mislead for features with many unique values.
Reproducible: a fixed random seed.
Few measured fluxes: for a year with few measured fluxes, a model trained on all years can fill that year.

title: Flux post-processing chain
text:
NoteSummary



diive processes the L1 fluxes in levels, from L2 (quality flags) to L4.2 (partitioning), with the notebook FluxPostProcessingChain.ipynb. Screened meteo data are used as drivers at L3.3, L4.1 and L4.2, and management data at L4.1 and, so far only as a reference, at L3.2.

text:

title: Flux post-processing chain
text:
Levels and flags

Guidelines: the chain follows community guidelines (Aubinet et al., 2012; Sabbatini et al., 2018).
Flags, not deletions: L2, L3.2 and L3.3 only create flags. No data are removed there.
Temporary QCF: after L2, the L2 flags remove rejected records before the outlier tests in L3.2.
Final QCF: L3.4 combines all flags. Gap-filling and partitioning use the filtered fluxes.
Three USTAR scenarios give three versions of NEE, N2O and CH4. See L3.3.

title: dataflow
text:
NoteSummary



dataflow uploads meteo logger files to the InfluxDB database automatically, as a command line script on the database server. dataflow reads each file with the settings of its filetype.



Steps: scans folders for files, assigns a filetype to each file it recognizes, reads the variables in the file and uploads the data.
Filetypes: each filetype is defined in a configuration file.
Database access: the connection settings are kept separate from the configuration files, for security.
Runs on: the database server, automatically. It is never run by hand.

Source code: github.com/holukas/dataflow

title: sonicread
text:
NoteSummary



sonicread logs the raw data of the sonic anemometer and the gas analyzers on site into one binary file per six hours, at 20 Hz. The files have no timestamps, variable names or units, and bico converts them to CSV files.


sonicread is a real-time logging script for eddy covariance raw data (Eugster & Plüss, 2010).

Output: binary raw data files, 20 Hz, one file per six hours. The start time of each file is in its file name.
Not in the files: timestamps, variable names and units. bico adds names and units when it converts the files to CSV.
Runs on: the data logger at the site.

The file format is described in EC raw data: sonicread.

title: rECord
text:
NoteSummary



rECord logs the raw data of the sonic anemometer and the gas analyzers on site into one CSV file per 30 min, at 20 Hz. It is an updated version of sonicread, in use since 2023, and its files need no conversion.
rECord (Robust Eddy Covariance Data Acquisition) is a logging script for eddy covariance raw data. It reads the sonic anemometer over a serial port, merges in the gas analyzer records and writes the combined records to files.

title: rECord
text:
Operation

Sonic anemometer: sets the timing. Each sonic record becomes one row in the file, at 20 Hz.
Supported sonics: Gill HS-50 and Gill R3-50.
Gas analyzers: a separate process reads each analyzer and passes its records to rECord. rECord puts each analyzer record into the row of the matching sonic record.
Missing analyzer records: replaced by the last valid record, up to a set number of times. After that the values are missing.
Status: one status column per analyzer marks rows where data were missing, repeated or discarded.
Files: a new file starts every 30 min at all sites. The finished file is then compressed.
Settings: two TOML files, one for rECord (variables, units, file format, instruments) and one with the settings sent to the sonic.

The file format is described in EC raw data: rECord.
Live view of the incoming data: ecvis, a terminal dashboard. The source code of rECord is not public.

title: EC raw data: sonicread
text:
NoteInfo



Eddy covariance raw data files are used to calculate preliminary (Level-0) and final fluxes (Level-1).

title: EC raw data: sonicread
section: EC raw data were recorded in real-time
text:
EC raw data were recorded in real-time
Eddy covariance (EC) raw data files are recorded using the custom-made real-time logging script sonicread (Eugster & Plüss, 2010). sonicread runs on a data logger and directly merges incoming raw data streams (20Hz or 10Hz) arriving from the instruments into one single file. Other loggers can easily be added to the datastream, creating complete data files comprising records from the sonic anemometer and any number of gas analyzers. Due to the real-time data merging of sonicread, it does not have to rely on any timestamps in the data files. This makes handling data from e.g. the QCL much easier, because the QCL logging software uses its own internal clock that is synchronized to the system clock of the QCL computer at regular intervals, and the QCL computer also has to be synchronized to the sonic/IRGA logger.

title: EC raw data: sonicread
text:
File format
Each EC raw data binary file contains a header section at the start of the file, followed by the data records of one installed sonic anemometer (SA) and one or more gas analyzers (GA). One raw data file comprises data over a time period of six hours. The files do not contain a timestamp, but the starting time of each file is written to the file name. Files do also not contain variable names or units. This info is later added during the file conversion using bico (see below).
The binary format of the data files is compressed and therefore irregularly structured. One line of data records (i.e., all records for a specific moment in time) can consist of a varying number of bytes and data columns. For example, if all data for all instruments are available at a specific timestamp, one line of data records consists of 26 bytes and 12 data columns. If the data for one instrument are missing, then one line of data records may only consist of 14 bytes and 8 data columns. An overview of data blocks, including their description, can be found online in the bico repository on GitHub here.
Data from the instruments arrive in data blocks at the logger. Because of the real-time nature of sonicread, all data blocks are stored to the same file in the moment they are recorded. The data blocks arrive sequentially: first the data block from instrument 1 (typically the sonic anemometer), then from instrument 2 (e.g., LI-7500), followed by other installed instruments (e.g., QCL or LGR). Data arriving from the sonic anemometer are the most reliable (SA runs most of the time) and most consistent (measurement frequency is always very close to the nominal 20Hz), therefore it is used as the “anchor” measurement for each file. This means that each data row starts with the sonic data, then additional data from other instruments are added.
The raw binary files lack any columnar structure or line breaks, presenting all instrument data blocks as a single, contiguous byte stream.
After the SA data block was stored to a file, the gas analyzer data that were available at that moment in time are added after the SA data block. If available, the data block of a second gas analyzer is added similarly. If no gas analyzer record is immediately available after the storing of the SA data block - for example when the GA is running at a lower time resolution such as 10Hz - the previous GA record is repeated. In the end, all files have a time resolution of 20Hz.
Whenever an instrument was added or removed at the site, the format of the raw binary files changed. For example, most of the time the regular structure of a raw binary file consists of (a) sonic data and (b) IRGA data. When a QCL system is installed at the site, the data of this new instrument are added to the sonic and IRGA data, e.g. after 6 columns of sonic data and 8 columns of IRGA data follow 5 columns of QCL data.
Time periods with different instrumental setup have to be calculated separately.

title: EC raw data: sonicread
text:
Creating regularly-structured files for EddyPro
EddyPro can handle regularly-structured binary files, but not irregularly-structured files. EddyPro needs to know in what sequence data are coming in, i.e. the sequence in which data are stored in a file.
Raw data files were converted to a regular structure (same number of columns for each line of records) using the script bico. During this conversion, the raw binary data are sorted into rows and columns, and at the end of one data row a line break is added. This means that one data row of records in the ASCII file consists of the data, sorted into columns, followed by a line break. Measured at 20Hz, there are 20 rows of data records per second. After the conversion, each data row has the same number of columns regardless of missing data, i.e., the data file becomes regularly-structured. Columns that contain no data have the value -9999 to mark missing values. This way, the files can be directly used in EddyPro for the flux calculations.
bico also adds additional information to the CSV files, such as the variable names for each column, and adds the respective units and the source instrument. In addition, bico converts the binary files to ASCII format (CSV). This is not strictly required by EddyPro, but it makes the files human-readable, which can be helpful in detecting data issues. To reduce the file size of the ASCII files, the CSV files were zipped (.gz). For flux calculations, the .gz files are first unzipped and then used in EddyPro using the home-made Python script fluxrun.
A typical name for a raw data file after the bico conversion is e.g. CH-CHA_202408091300.csv.gz, whereby the time info in the file name gives the starting time for the data.

title: EC raw data: sonicread
section: Example structure of EC binary raw data files
text:
Example structure of EC binary raw data files
This example describes the structure of a binary raw data file with data from 1 sonic anemometer and 2 different gas analyzers (open-path LI-7500 and LGR).

HEADER (29 bytes): Contains information created by the logging script sonicread. This information is not written to the regular ASCII file, but it is written to the bico log file during conversion from binary to ASCII. Each of the irregular binary files contains this header section.
INSTRUMENT 1: Data block coming from sonic anemometer Solent R3-50 (R350-B): 12 bytes (big endian short integer).
INSTRUMENT 2: Data block coming from Li-7500 (IRGA75-A): 2-16 bytes. In case of 2 bytes, data from the IRGA are missing. 16 bytes means all data available.
INSTRUMENT 3: Data block coming from the LGR laser (LGR-A): 2-33 bytes. In case of 2 bytes, data from the LGR are missing. 33 bytes means all data available

Each full data record (one row of data records for a specific moment in time) within the file occupies 61 bytes, consisting of 12 bytes for the SA data, 16 bytes for IRGA data, and 33 bytes for LGR data. If IRGA data are missing, the record size reduces to 47 bytes (12 bytes SA data, 2 bytes for missing IRGA data, 33 bytes LGR data). Conversely, if LGR data are missing, the record size is 30 bytes (12 bytes SA data, 16 bytes IRGA data, 2 bytes for missing LGR data). A 29-byte header is present at the start of the file, preceding the data records.

title: Flux Processing Guide
text:
NoteSummary



This guide describes the chain from raw eddy covariance and meteo data to quality-controlled fluxes and the flux product. The chart shows each step as a numbered box that links to its page.
Numbers in brackets refer to the boxes in the chart.

title: Flux Processing Guide
text:
Time resolution
The pills at the bottom of the boxes show the time resolution of the data.

Eddy covariance raw data: 20 Hz. The fluxes calculated from them are 30 min, from L0 on.
Meteo data: high resolution in the logger files, the upload and the raw bucket: mostly 1 min, sometimes 10 s or 30 min.
From the meteo screening on: 30 min. The screening resamples the data.

title: Flux Processing Guide
text:
Eddy covariance

Raw data logging (1, 2): a logging script on the data logger at the site records the raw data at 20 Hz.

sonicread writes binary files (1). Format: EC raw data: sonicread.
rECord writes CSV files in TOA5 format (2). Format: EC raw data: rECord.

Raw data conversion (3, 16): bico converts the binary files from sonicread to CSV files.

Files from rECord are already CSV files and skip this step.

L0 · Preliminary run (4, 5): fluxrun runs EddyPro on the raw CSV files, with relaxed settings and a wide time lag window.

The preliminary fluxes are used for checks: complete data, plausible fluxes, time lags, wind direction.
They are used to refine the settings for L1, e.g. the time lag.

L1 · Final flux run (6, 7): the final fluxrun run, with the refined settings, on the same raw data.

It also uses 6 meteo variables as input (17).
The result is the EddyPro output, 30 min. All later steps use it.

title: Flux Processing Guide
text:
Meteo

Meteo logging (8): meteo stations on site record the meteo data.
Meteo upload (9, 10): dataflow uploads the logger files to the raw bucket of the InfluxDB database.
Meteo screening (11, 12): a diive notebook screens the meteo data, resamples them to 30 min and uploads them to the processed bucket.
Meteo for EddyPro (17): a diive notebook formats 6 screened meteo variables for the L1 run.
Additional meteo for dataset (18): diive notebooks merge the screened meteo data from both screening tools, correct them on the 30-min data and write them for the dataset.

They are drivers for the diive flux post-processing chain.
They also go into the flux product.

title: Flux Processing Guide
text:
Management

Management data (15): field records.

Used at L3.2 (outlier flagging) and L4.1 (gap-filling).
Go into the flux product, if relevant.

title: Flux Processing Guide
text:
Flux processing

Flux post-processing chain (13): the notebook FluxPostProcessingChain.ipynb processes the L1 fluxes from L2 to L4.2.

Meteo drivers are used at L3.3 (USTAR threshold), L4.1 (gap-filling) and L4.2 (partitioning).

Flux product (14): fluxes, meteo data and management data.

title: Flux Processing Guide
text:
Scripts

sonicread logs eddy covariance raw data on site as binary files.
rECord logs eddy covariance raw data on site as CSV files.
bico converts the binary raw data written by sonicread to CSV files for EddyPro.
fluxrun runs EddyPro on the raw data files, converted by bico or written directly by rECord.
dataflow finds logger files, assigns a filetype and uploads the data to the database.
diive screens the meteo data and runs the flux post-processing chain.

title: L1 · Final flux run

text:
Before the L1 run
Needed for the L1 run:

Tips:

One folder: the OPENLAG results, the meteo file, the .eddypro and the .metadata file are kept in one folder.
Meaningful names: e.g. <SITE>_<YEAR>_[IRGA75]_R350-A_IRGA75-A.eddypro: site, year, the gas analyzer the settings are for, then the instruments in the order of the columns in the raw data files (sonic first).
Same name: the .metadata file has the same name as the .eddypro file.
Saving: in the EddyPro interface, “Save” saves the .eddypro file only. The .metadata file is saved automatically.
Archive: the .eddypro and .metadata files of each run are stored with the dataset.
Periods: setups change over the years. One settings file is used per period with the same setup, e.g. two runs in a year in which the gas analyzer was replaced.

title: L1 · Final flux run
text:
Time lags

IRGA (CO2, H2O): covariance maximization in a narrow window around the nominal lag. Without a clear covariance peak in the window, EddyPro uses the nominal lag.
QCL and LGR (N2O, CH4): a constant lag, per year or per period in which the lag changed.
Window: typically from 0 s to 5 s if the lag stays below 5 s, otherwise to 10 s. The minimum can be negative.
Setting location: nominal lag, minimum and maximum per gas in the raw file description (Metadata).

title: L1 · Final flux run
text:
Open-path IRGA

Closed-path IRGA (e.g. LI-7200): the fluxes do not change after L1.
Open-path IRGA (e.g. LI-7500): CO2 fluxes may need a correction for the self-heating of the sensor, after L1. It is not part of the chart.
Self-heating correction in EddyPro (off-season uptake correction, Burba et al., 2008): not used. It was developed for vertically mounted instruments and does not account for an inclined IRGA, e.g. tilted by 15°. The self-heating effect of an inclined IRGA is assumed to be much smaller. In a comparison with parallel closed-path fluxes, the EddyPro correction performed poorly.
Conditions: the correction was developed for cold conditions, mainly below -10 °C.
Without parallel measurements: applying the correction is risky, because its effect cannot be checked. With a closed-path IRGA next to the open-path one, the correction can be scaled to match it (Kittler et al., 2017).
Gap-filling: gap-filling uncorrected open-path fluxes amplifies too high uptake.

title: L1 · Final flux run
text:
Checks after the L1 run

Output folder: fluxrun created it.
Data availability: the plot shows no unexpected gaps.
Flux files: the _fluxnet_ and _full_output_ files exist. Only .tmp versions mean that the run failed.
Spectral assessment file: it exists. Without it, EddyPro fell back to Moncrieff et al. (1997), e.g. because the period was too short.
Number of spectra: the fluxrun log lists the binned spectra available for the spectral correction. It can be low for N2O and CH4.
Spectral correction factor (SCF): mostly between 1 and 2. Closed-path analyzers with an inlet have higher values than open-path IRGAs.
Output: fluxes, wind speed and direction, time lags, unexpected gaps.

When the SCF is too high, e.g. 2.5 to 5 for N2O or CH4, the spectral correction did not work:

The ensemble (co)spectra in the spectral analysis output of EddyPro are checked.
Periods with different instruments are run separately.
Faulty instruments are a possible cause, e.g. a broken sonic distorts the cospectra.
With too few records for unstable conditions, that threshold is lowered in EddyPro.

title: L1 · Final flux run
text:
Known issues

Empty SSITC flags in _fluxnet_ files: EddyPro before v7.0.7 wrote empty SSITC flags to the _fluxnet_ file. It was fixed in EddyPro v7.0.7 and fluxrun v1.0. The _full_output_ files are not affected; there the flags are called qc_<flux>. For older years, the _full_output_ files are used.
Flag check: how many records each flag removes. The SSITC flag usually removes a lot, e.g. 25 %. A flag that removes 0 % stands out.

title: L1 · Final flux run
text:
Older fluxes

Settings change: fluxes calculated years ago used older software and settings that are not necessarily the best today.
Metadata of old years can be estimated, e.g. separations measured on old photos, or an uncertain sonic orientation.
Before reuse: how the fluxes were calculated is checked, and whether the older years should be reprocessed.

title: L0 · Preliminary run
text:
NoteSummary



fluxrun runs EddyPro with relaxed settings and without meteo input, and the preliminary fluxes are used to check the data. The L0 run in preparation for the L1 final flux run is called OPENLAG run: with a wide time lag window and no default lag, it shows the range of the found time lags, which is used to set a narrow time lag window for L1.

title: L0 · Preliminary run
text:
Reasons for L0

Not everything is ready during the year: e.g. the screened meteo data for EddyPro are not available yet.
The spectral correction needs a long period: at least several months, especially for Fratini et al. (2012), which also uses RH classes.
A test run: if L0 gives reasonable fluxes with relaxed settings, the data are most likely OK.
Settings for L1: once the year is complete, the L0 results help to set up the L1 run.

title: L0 · Preliminary run
text:
No strict rules

L0 has no fixed settings. They depend on what is checked. Different settings are tried to see how they affect the fluxes.
Some settings may not be final yet, e.g. the vertical separation of the gas analyzer.
A faster spectral correction saves time: Moncrieff et al. (1997) instead of Fratini et al. (2012) or Horst (1997).
Minimal output is enough.

See L0 and L1 compared for the differences.

title: L0 · Preliminary run
text:
Use of the L0 fluxes

Site check: complete data and plausible fluxes.
Time lags: the nominal lag and the time lag window for the L1 run.
Wind direction: comparison of the wind direction across years.

title: L0 · Preliminary run
text:
Time lags (OPENLAG)
An L0 run can have many purposes. The L0 run in preparation for L1 is called OPENLAG run, because it searches the time lag in a wide window without a default lag. The “true” time lag has to be known before the fluxes of a year are finalized. The OPENLAG run shows whether a clear lag can be found, and whether it stays in a similar range over the period.

When: before every L1 run, and always when it is not known where the lag lies, e.g. for a new instrument.
Time lag compensation: “Covariance maximization”, without a default. EddyPro then writes the lag it really found, with no fallback value.
No nominal lag.
Wide window: typically 0 to 10 s. Windows from -5 to +20 s have also been used. There are no rules.
Minimum: 0 s or negative. With a start value of 0 s, EddyPro started the lag search later, e.g. at +1 s; -1 s avoids that.
Maximum: 10 s or 20 s. A long inlet line of a closed-path analyzer can need more, but a lag of 20 s would be unusual.
Narrow down: if the lags cluster in a smaller range, a second OPENLAG run with a narrower window gives a clearer peak.


Finding the nominal lag

L0 flux: checked first for plausibility.
Lags: e.g. co2_time_lag in the EddyPro _full_output_ file.
Heatmap: during daytime, the lag should be found at a similar place.
Histogram with one bin per possible lag: EddyPro writes lags in steps of 0.05 s, so the number of bins is (maximum lag - minimum lag) / 0.05 + 1, e.g. 201 bins for 0 to 10 s. With fewer or more bins, different lags are pooled into one bin.
Edge bins: not used, because lags pile up at the window limits when no clear lag was found.
Peak bin: read with two decimals, zoomed in. The peak is the nominal lag for L1.


IRGA (CO2, H2O): the L1 run uses the peak as nominal lag, with a narrow window around it.
QCL and LGR (N2O, CH4): the L1 run uses the peak as a constant lag, without a window.
Different gases: each gas can have its own lag. The lag of passive gases (CO2, CH4, N2O) does not depend on the weather. The lag of H2O depends strongly on relative humidity, so in closed-path analyzers it is generally longer than that of CO2.
Two peaks: a histogram with two peaks means that the lag changed. The data are then split into periods, each with its own lag.
Drifting lags: with very low fluxes, e.g. N2O and CH4, the lag can drift over time. dyco detects and removes time lags in the raw data (Vitale et al., 2024).



Window size
From the EddyPro help:

Too narrow: the actual lag often lies outside the window. EddyPro then often uses the default or a window limit. This leads to systematic flux underestimation.
Too wide: unrealistic lags are found more often, especially when the covariance is small and varies erratically with the lag. This often leads to flux overestimation.



Automatic time lag optimization

Method: EddyPro estimates the window and the default lag itself, for H2O in RH classes.
Not recommended: at one site it gave unrealistic CO2 lags. The likely reason: the logger buffers records, e.g. 20 records (1 s), and EddyPro, which estimates the lag from the flow rate, does not know about that buffer.
Leaving the nominal lag at 0: EddyPro then calculates it from the tube length and the flow rate. This gives e.g. about 0.15 s, far below lags found in OPENLAG runs, e.g. 1.25 s. Different lag settings can explain differences between flux datasets.

title: L0 · Preliminary run
text:
Wind direction

The histogram of the wind direction of each year is compared with a reference period.
The offset is the number of degrees to add to the wind direction of a year to get the histogram closest to the reference.
Small offsets across all years mean that the orientation of the sonic anemometer stayed the same.

text:
Steps

Merge: the two versions into one series.
Corrections: on the merged 30-min series.

title: Additional meteo for dataset
text:
Corrections on the 30-min data
Some data need corrections that can only be made on the 30-min data, after the meteo screening. Problems that span years, sensors or data sources, or that need a reference series at 30 min, show up in the merged 30-min record.

Logger clock errors: a shifted block of timestamps. A heatmap of the daily cycle shows the shift: after the correction, e.g. the warmest hours have to be around midday again. A clock error affects every variable of that logger.
Damaged periods: compared with a reference sensor, e.g. on the same tower or at a nearby station, day by day. Periods that cannot be repaired are removed and then gap-filled.
Sensor or logger changes: a replaced sensor can make the series step at the changeover. A reference series that spans the change shows the step and gives the correction. The measured series is kept and a homogenized one is added.
Gap-filling per period: no gap-filling model is trained across a sensor change.
Flags: for filled values, e.g. FLAG_<variable>_ISFILLED, and the source of each value, e.g. FLAG_<variable>_SOURCE.
Resolution check: the data must really be 30 min.

title: Additional meteo for dataset
text:
Preparing the drivers

Gap-filling: drivers need complete time series, e.g. gap-filled with XGBoost in diive, with lagged variants as additional features.
VPD: calculated from gap-filled TA and RH.
Lagged variants: e.g. the mean over the preceding 3 hours (MEAN3H), and that mean shifted back in steps of 3 hours.
Time since precipitation: the number of records since the last precipitation event.
Sensor changes: when sensors or depths changed without overlap, the most similar series are merged.

text:

Drivers for the flux post-processing chain, at L3.3 (USTAR threshold), L4.1 (gap-filling) and L4.2 (partitioning).
Flux product: the meteo data go into it.

title: Sharing with FLUXNET
text:
NoteSummary



The L1 fluxes and the meteo data are uploaded to FLUXNET through the European Fluxes Database Cluster (EFDC), with metadata in BADM files. FLUXNET then runs the outlier removal, USTAR filtering, gap-filling and partitioning with its own scripts.

title: Sharing with FLUXNET
text:
Upload content

L1 fluxes: not outlier-removed, not USTAR-filtered, not gap-filled, not partitioned. FLUXNET does these steps with its own scripts. See L1.
Clearly wrong data: set to -9999 before the upload, e.g. fluxes from a defective sensor that still produced data, or periods with low signal strength (“soft QC”).
Flux variables: from the EddyPro output, renamed to FLUXNET codes. Only the most relevant variables, not all of them.
The EddyPro *_fluxnet_* file cannot be uploaded as it is, despite its name. For older years, that file has empty SSITC flags.
Meteo data: from the meteo files, not from the EddyPro output, which has meteo values only where fluxes were calculated. See Meteo for EddyPro.
BADM files: metadata about the site and the variables go with the upload.

FLUXNET calls the uploaded data Level-2: original data from the PI, checked or filtered only for out-of-range values or clearly wrong data. FLUXNET Level-2 is the L1 of this guide.

title: Raw and processed data
text:
NoteSummary



Raw data are files generated directly by sensors and loggers. Any change to raw data, e.g. gap-filling or a flux calculation, makes them processed data.

title: Raw and processed data
text:
Raw data
Raw data files are copied from the site to a central storage, where they are sorted into their destination folders.

title: Raw and processed data
text:
Processed data
Raw data are used to generate processed data.
Some examples:

When the air temperature time series has many gaps and is gap-filled, the gap-filled time series is processed data.
Data from the sonic anemometers and gas analyzers (raw data) are used to calculate eddy covariance fluxes (processed data).

In this guide, the eddy covariance raw data are described in EC raw data: sonicread and EC raw data: rECord. The meteo data are kept in the database in a raw bucket and, after screening, in a processed bucket.

title: diive
text:
NoteSummary



diive is a Python library for time series processing of eddy covariance and meteo data. In this guide, its notebooks screen the meteo data, prepare meteo data for EddyPro and the dataset, and run the flux post-processing chain.


The library covers quality control, outlier detection, gap-filling and flux partitioning.
In this guide, diive is used in notebooks:

DatabaseInfluxStepwiseMeteoScreening.ipynb: meteo screening.
FormatMeteoForEddyProFluxProcessing.ipynb: meteo data for the L1 final flux run (biomet data).
DatabaseInfluxDownloadSpecificVars.ipynb and DatabaseInfluxDownloadAllVarsOfMeasurements.ipynb: meteo data as drivers for the flux post-processing chain and for the flux product.
FluxPostProcessingChain.ipynb: the flux post-processing chain, from L2 to L4.2.

The notebooks that read from or write to the database need the configs and configs_secret folders.

Install: pip install diive, with pip install "diive[db]" for the database notebooks.
Runs on: a local installation, on demand.

Source code: github.com/holukas/diive · Documentation: diive.readthedocs.io

title: bico
text:
NoteSummary



bico converts the binary raw data files from sonicread to CSV files with a regular format that EddyPro can read. It adds variable names and units and writes one CSV file per raw data file.


Raw data files from rECord are already CSV files and skip the conversion.

Input: binary raw data files from sonicread, 20 Hz.
Output: one CSV file per raw data file with a 3-row header, optionally gzip-compressed.
Regular format: EddyPro needs every row to have the same number of values. The binary files from sonicread are irregular.
Readable: unlike the binary files, the CSV files are human-readable.
Data-block specs: a data-block spec for each instrument describes its byte layout, and bico decodes every file into labelled columns. Sonic anemometers and gas analyzers (IRGA, QCL, LGR) are supported.
Also writes: per-file statistics, optional plots, a log and a copy of the settings used, all in one output folder per run.
Runs on: a local installation, automatically from the command line, and on demand with a terminal interface when the fluxes are finalized.

bico is built for the binary format of the ETH Grassland Sciences group, not as a general converter. The format itself is described in EC raw data: sonicread.
Source code and installation: github.com/holukas/bico

title: fluxrun
text:
NoteSummary



fluxrun is a Python wrapper for EddyPro that handles the files, checks and plots around the flux calculation. It runs the L0 preliminary run and the L1 final flux run on the raw data CSV files.
fluxrun uses EddyPro v7.0.9, which calculates the fluxes from the raw data.

title: fluxrun
text:
Input

Raw data CSV files, from bico (3-row header) or rECord (4-row header), compressed (.gz) or not.
An EddyPro settings file (.eddypro) with a .metadata file of the same name next to it.

The raw data files are usually stored compressed (.gz), because compression makes them much smaller. They come compressed from two places:

bico can compress the CSV files it writes when it converts the binary files from sonicread.
rECord records CSV files and then compresses them.

fluxrun decompresses the .gz files itself during the flux calculation, so they don’t need to be unpacked first.

title: fluxrun
text:
Two runs

L0 · Preliminary run: gives preliminary fluxes, with relaxed settings and a wide time lag window. They are used for checks and to refine the settings, e.g. the time lag. See L0.
L1 · Final flux run: the final run with the refined settings, on the same raw data. It also uses the screened meteo data (biomet data), formatted for EddyPro with the diive notebook FormatMeteoForEddyProFluxProcessing.ipynb. See L1.

title: fluxrun
text:
Features

Finds the raw data files by file name pattern and date range, and skips empty files.
Decompresses .gz files into the run’s output folder, and can delete the decompressed files afterwards.
Replaces non-numeric values with -9999, the missing value EddyPro expects in the raw data files.
Runs EddyPro’s raw processing, then its flux computation and correction.
Plots raw data availability, raw data aggregates and a summary of the EddyPro output.
Writes everything to one output folder per run, named with a run ID (FR-YYYYMMdd-HHMMSS), with a main log and a log of warnings and errors.
Runs on: a local installation, automatically throughout the year for the L0 runs, and on demand with a graphical interface or from the command line.

title: fluxrun
text:
Tips

More output than EddyPro alone: e.g. the complete EddyPro log, which shows problems such as the fallback of the spectral correction.
File name pattern: the pattern uses placeholders for the date and time, e.g. yyyy, mm, dd, HH, MM. The extension must be right, because .gz files are decompressed first.
Start and end: refer to the date and time in the file names, not to the half-hourly fluxes. Start and end are both included.
Year boundary: a six-hour sonicread file that starts in the evening of 31 December also holds the first hours of the next year. That file is also copied to the source folder of the next year’s run.
Run without EddyPro: switching off the flux calculation still checks which files are found and plots their availability.
Decompressed files: need a lot of disk space. fluxrun can delete them after the run, unless they are needed, e.g. for the L1 run after an OPENLAG run.
Settings: saved when the run starts, also to the output folder of the run.
Versions: fluxrun is updated with new EddyPro versions and bug fixes. The log shows the fluxrun version, e.g. to check for the empty SSITC flags of older versions.

title: fluxrun
text:
Output
The EddyPro fluxnet output file (30 min) goes on to the diive flux post-processing chain.
Source code and installation: github.com/holukas/fluxrun

title: L4.2 · Partitioning

NoteSummary



L4.2 partitions NEE into GPP and RECO, using the gap-filled NEE from L4.1 and the meteo drivers. The daytime method (Lasslop et al., 2010) is generally preferred, with the nighttime method (Reichstein et al., 2005) for comparison.



NEE: partitioned into GPP and RECO.
ET: partitioned into its components.
Methods: the daytime method (Lasslop et al., 2010) is generally preferred. The nighttime method (Reichstein et al., 2005) is also run, and the results are compared.

title: QCF: overall quality flag
text:
NoteSummary



The QCF combines the flags of single quality tests into one overall flag per record: 0 best, 1 OK, 2 bad. The same logic applies to flux and meteo data, and L3.4 builds the final QCF of the fluxes.

title: QCF: overall quality flag
text:
Test flags
Each single test gives a flag: 0 passed, 1 moderate quality, 2 failed.

Hard flags: tests that give only 0 or 2. The test is so important that a failed test makes the record bad, whatever the other tests say.
Soft flags: tests that can give 1. A record with one or two of them can still be OK for some analyses.

title: Management data
text:
NoteSummary



Field records of the site management are turned into 30-min time series of the events and of the time since each event, which go into the flux product, if relevant. The series have been used for gap-filling with tree-based models in L4.1, and in L3.2 so far only to find the management dates and check whether outlier removal around them made sense.

title: Management data
text:
Use of the data

L4.1 (gap-filling): used in the past as features for tree-based models, e.g. random forest.
L3.2 (outlier flagging): meant to be used here. So far, only to find where management took place and whether outlier removal around those dates made sense.
Flux product, if relevant.

title: Management data
section: From field records to a time series
text:
From field records to a time series
Tree-based gap-filling models in L4.1 need the management as a time series.

Events: each kind of event gets a variable name, e.g. MGMT_MOWING, MGMT_FERT_ORG, MGMT_GRAZING. Similar events are grouped.
Daily time series: one column per event, 1 on days with the event, 0 otherwise. Whole days, because exact start and end times are often missing.
Time since the event: for each event, the time since its last occurrence is counted, e.g. TIMESINCE_MGMT_MOWING. This puts each record in relation to past events.
Half-hourly: convert the daily data to 30 min, with TIMESTAMP_MIDDLE.
Several fields: if the footprint covers fields with different management, the wind direction is used to pick the field the wind comes from, e.g. _FOOTPRINT variables.

title: L2 · Quality flag expansion
text:
NoteSummary



L2 expands the quality flags of the EddyPro output into separate test flags, e.g. for steady state, completeness of the raw data and signal strength. Only flags are added, and no data are removed.

title: L2 · Quality flag expansion
text:
Flags
Each test gets its own flag: 0 highest quality, 1 moderate quality, 2 low quality.








Test
Checks
Applied to




SSITC
steady state and developed turbulence (Foken and Wichura, 1996; Mauder and Foken, 2006), from the EddyPro output
all fluxes


Gas completeness
how complete the 20 Hz gas data are: 0 above 99 %, 1 97 to 99 %, 2 below 97 % (Sabbatini et al., 2018)
all fluxes


Spectral correction factor
out-of-range correction factors: 0 below 2, 1 2 to 4, 2 4 and above (Sabbatini et al., 2018)
all fluxes


Signal strength
the signal strength of the IRGA, above or below a set value
IRGA fluxes (CO2, H2O)


Raw data screening
spikes, amplitude resolution and drop-outs in the 20 Hz data (Vickers and Mahrt, 1997), from the EddyPro output
all fluxes


Angle of attack
unrealistic vertical wind from the sonic anemometer
optional, e.g. for periods with a faulty sonic




Signal strength: for open-path IRGAs, a high value of the automatic gain control (AGC) means a poor signal. For (en)closed-path IRGAs it is usually the other way round.

EddyPro does not use the AGC in the flux calculation. It is only used here, in the quality control.
The AGC is logged in steps of 6.25 %. The value for the best signal differs between instruments and can change, e.g. from 50 % to 43.75 % after a change inside the instrument. The best-signal value of each instrument has to be known.
The flag rejects records above a set value, e.g. 80 % or 90 %.

Empty SSITC flags: the number of records each flag removes shows empty flags. See known issues in L1.
Hard and soft flags: some tests give only 0 or 2. See QCF.

title: L2 · Quality flag expansion
text:
Temporary QCF

The L2 flags are combined into a first QCF.
It removes the rejected records before the outlier tests in L3.2, so that they run on data that passed L2.
It is not the final QCF. That one is built in L3.4. See QCF.

title: Meteo for EddyPro
text:
Use in EddyPro

SW_IN and LW_IN: the “multiple regression” version of the off-season uptake correction (Burba et al., 2008).
PPFD: day and night radiation load on the instrument surface. The off-season uptake correction uses it to pick its coefficients and to model the instrument surface temperature.
RH, TA and PA: replace the mean values that EddyPro would otherwise estimate from the eddy covariance data or from the site characteristics.
TA: also used, for example, in the WPL correction for IRGA75.

Source: EddyPro v7.0 manual.

title: Meteo for EddyPro
text:
Corrections first
The 6 variables need the same corrections on the 30-min data as the additional meteo for dataset, e.g. for logger clock errors or sensor changes, before they go to EddyPro.

title: Meteo for EddyPro
text:
The meteo file
A CSV file with two header rows, variable names and units, e.g.:
date,time,Lwin_1_1_1,PPFD_1_1_1,RH_1_1_1,Rg_1_1_1,Ta_1_1_1,Pa_1_1_1
yyyy-mm-dd,HH:MM,W+1m-2,umol+1m-2s-1,%,W+1m-2,C,kPa
2020-01-01,00:30,309.09,0.019,100,3.56,-0.10,98.64

Quality-controlled: all 6 variables come from the meteo screening.
All 6 columns: a column stays in the file even if the variable is missing completely, filled with -9999.
Missing values: -9999 (or -9999.0).
Timestamp: date and time without seconds.
Units: checked, especially for PA (Pa, hPa or kPa). See the 6 variables for the units EddyPro accepts.
Names: EddyPro names, e.g. Rg for SW_IN, because the EddyPro interface only offers global radiation.
Text editor: the file is checked in a text editor. Excel can change the format when it opens the file.
Extending a file: a file from previous years can be extended with the new data.

title: Meteo for EddyPro
text:
Import check in EddyPro

With a wrong format, EddyPro does not stop. It ignores the file and uses its own estimates instead, with no clear warning.
The fluxrun log shows the line 1 biomet record(s) imported. once per half-hour.

title: Meteo for EddyPro
text:
Notes

Gap-filled input: gap-filled variables, e.g. SW_IN, TA and PPFD, give EddyPro a complete meteo input.
Missing variables: without data for a variable, e.g. RH, EddyPro estimates it from the eddy covariance data or the site characteristics. See use in EddyPro.
Missing PA: with PA set to -9999, EddyPro calculates a constant pressure from the site altitude. Pressure measured in the IRGA box is an alternative that varies over the year. In one test, the two options gave minor differences in the cumulative CO2 and H2O fluxes.
Meteo in the EddyPro output: EddyPro writes the meteo variables only for records with flux results. Meteo data for sharing, e.g. with FLUXNET, are not taken from the EddyPro output.
